body.text: The 2026 US midterm elections are less than four weeks away, and the political environment is becoming increasingly difficult for Donald Trump’s Republican Party. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats will be up for election on November 3.

Polling increasingly points to Democratic gains in the House, while the Senate race remains more uncertain. Economic dissatisfaction, rising energy costs and the political fallout from the Iran conflict are putting pressure on the Republican Party.

This does not necessarily make 2026 an exceptional election. Historically, the President’s party tends to lose congressional seats in midterm elections. Since 1938, the President’s party has lost House ground in 20 of 22 midterm elections. In fact, during Trump’s first midterms in 2018, Republicans lost 41 seats in the House. It’s a vulnerability Trump is well aware of.

What is particularly interesting about the 2026 US midterm elections is that Republican candidates in 41 of the 62 competitive congressional races have sought to distance themselves from President Donald Trump, according to a Reuters review, amid concerns over electoral implications of his policies. The Iran conflict, rising fuel prices, data centres and beef imports have emerged as points of contention.

Republican unease with Trump has become visible not only in campaign strategy but also in congressional action. Some members of his party have joined efforts to limit his war powers, challenged the administration over the release of Epstein-related files, and aspects of tariff policies, including those affecting Canada.

Republican candidates have also reduced Trump’s visibility in their campaigns by removing his endorsements from their websites and avoiding joint appearances. Again, such distancing is not unprecedented; Republicans adopted similar strategies during the 2018 midterm elections. However, the 2026 midterms stand out for the breadth of the distancing and the range of policy disagreements involved.

With Trump’s approval ratings remaining weak, his early campaign stops have also drawn attention. Rather than prioritising competitive districts that could determine control of Congress, he has been holding rallies in Republican strongholds such as Texas, Oklahoma, and Alabama.
What will the midterms mean for Trump’s power?

If Democrats regain control of the House while Republicans retain the Senate, as it happened after the 2018 midterm elections, the immediate consequences would likely centre on increased congressional oversight rather than a fundamental reversal of Trump’s foreign policy. Democrats could hold hearings, demand documents, and investigate the legal, humanitarian, and migration-related implications of the administration’s policies, including the costs and legal basis of military operations. They could also use the appropriations process to seek restrictions or conditions on military funding, although such measures would face obstacles in the Senate and could be subject to a presidential veto.
Impeachment proceedings could also re-emerge, but convicting Trump and removing him from office would require the support of two-thirds of the senators present.

The balance of power would change more substantially, however, if Democrats gained control of both chambers. A Democratic Senate could complicate the passage of legislation and funding measures and make confirmation of future presidential nominees more difficult. However, this possibility remains highly uncertain. Assuming they retain their current seats, Democrats would need a net gain of at least four seats to secure a 51-seat Senate majority.
Can MAGA remain a unifying force within the GOP after Trump?
The 2026 midterms could provide an early indication of the challenges MAGA (Make America Great Again) may face in maintaining its cohesion beyond Trump.

The MAGA movement is a populist, nationalist faction within the broader Republican Party wing that centres on Donald Trump’s “America First” agenda, which prioritises economic protectionism through tariffs, strict anti-immigration policies, scepticism towards foreign intervention, and a disruptive anti-establishment posture. Trump’s MAGA movement has indeed united a diverse coalition of economic nationalists, immigration hardliners, religious conservatives, and anti-establishment voters within the Republican Party—often referred to as Grand Old Party (GOP)—whose priorities do not always align.

However, growing dissatisfaction with aspects of Trump’s policy record, alongside his declining popularity and efforts by an increasing number of Republican candidates to distance themselves from him ahead of the 2026 midterms point to growing tensions within the GOP. And with the Constitution barring Trump from being elected to another presidential term in 2028, the question of succession becomes increasingly significant.

The question, therefore, is whether MAGA can retain its cohesion under new leadership or whether competing factions will emerge, each claiming to represent the true heir to “America First”. Trump’s departure could expose differences within the coalition that his leadership has held together. Such fragmentation, if it occurs, would not necessarily signal a decline in MAGA’s broader political influence. The evolution of earlier conservative movements, such as the Tea Party, offers a useful historical reference, illustrating how a movement’s ideas can continue to shape the Republican Party even as it loses its distinct organisational identity.
Girisanker S.B. Nair is a Research Faculty at the Indian Council of World Affairs (ICWA), a New Delhi-based think-tank, specialising in US, Latin American, and Caribbean studies.
